The evidence clusters into conflicting outcomes: d1, d4, and d5 report positive or neutral effects on specific cognitive skills (attention, executive functions), while d2 and d6 associate gaming (especially addiction) with negative cognitive impacts. d3 and d7 present mixed results within themselves (e.g., better inhibitory control but lower empathy). Research on video games and cognitive skills shows conflicting outcomes. Some studies report positive associations, such as improved attention, visual processing, and executive functions from playing specific games, particularly action video games [d1, d4, d5]. Other research links video game addiction to worse memory, attention, and cognitive skills in children [d2], and some sources claim negative effects on brain structure and memory [d6]. Individual studies also present mixed results, noting limited negative impacts on some social-cognitive skills but positive effects on others like inhibitory control [d3, d7]. Therefore, the overall evidence does not support a uniform negative impact; the relationship appears complex and depends on factors like game genre, play patterns, and individual differences.
